question: A 30-year-old man with a pelvic fracture and two long-bone fractures is in haemorrhagic shock. Damage control resuscitation (DCR) is initiated. Which blood product ratio best reflects current DCR practice?

answers.text: Packed red cells only, targeting Hb ≥10 g/dL before any plasma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the old 'crystalloid-first, blood products-later' approach. DCR replaced this because aggressive crystalloid resuscitation worsens coagulopathy, hypothermia, and acidosis — the lethal triad.

answers.text: Packed red cells : Fresh frozen plasma : Platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. DCR targets a 1:1:1 ratio of PRBC:FFP:Platelets, mimicking whole blood. This haemostatic resuscitation strategy prevents dilutional coagulopathy. Permissive hypotension (MAP 50 mmHg, SBP 80–90 mmHg) is maintained until surgical haemostasis.

answers.text: Packed red cells : Fresh frozen plasma in a 4:1 ratio

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A 4:1 ratio was used historically and leads to dilutional coagulopathy. Current evidence (PROPPR trial) supports 1:1:1.

answers.text: Crystalloid (normal saline 2 L) bolus first, then blood products if no response

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Large-volume saline boluses cause hyperchloraemic acidosis, dilutional coagulopathy, and worsened outcomes. DCR principles limit crystalloid use and prioritise early haemostatic blood product resuscitation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review DCR: the key principle is early 1:1:1 blood products (PRBC:FFP:Plt), permissive hypotension until surgical bleeding control, and minimising crystalloid to avoid the lethal triad.

Correct. 1:1:1 DCR is standard of care for haemorrhagic shock. Remember the lethal triad: coagulopathy + hypothermia + acidosis — DCR addresses all three by replacing the permissive-hypotension + haemostatic resuscitation strategy.
